sampling_model.design: Let \(G_{\mathrm{obs}}=(M,E_{\mathrm{obs}})\) record exactly the observed paired cross-covariance blocks in addition to every view marginal. For each edge \(\{a,b\}\in E_{\mathrm{obs}}\), one source supplies independent and identically distributed centered Gaussian paired observations of \((X^{(a)},X^{(b)})\). For every \(a\in M\), a marginal source supplies independent and identically distributed centered Gaussian observations of \(X^{(a)}\). Every edge-joint covariance and every marginal covariance is positive definite.
sampling_model.units: Observations are independent and identically distributed within each edge or marginal source, and all sources have the corresponding edge or marginal law of the same target \(P\). No independence between different sources is assumed; samples may share units, and the simultaneous guarantee uses only sourcewise concentration and a union bound.
sampling_model.treatment: There is no treatment variable; the causal target is the shared-order structural coefficient family and its invariant ancestry.
sampling_model.overlap: Alignment is required only within each observed edge sample. No nonedge cross-view block is used. The fixed graph-feasibility margin is strictly positive, so laws on residual-diagonality or positive-definite-completion boundaries are excluded from exact order exclusion. Signal-dependent selection, population transport, and source-specific target laws remain outside the model.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Empirical covariance blocks are estimated separately from the edge and marginal sources, with multiplicity \(\lvert E_{\mathrm{obs}}\rvert+m\). Modified-Cholesky coefficients, observed-edge residual violations, coordinatewise completion margins, and Schur states are recomputed for every moment collection in the simultaneous operator-norm region.

body.tldr: On the restrictive component-aligned Gaussian LiMVAM class, a candidate common order is compatible with an arbitrary observed view graph exactly when every observed-edge residual cross-block is diagonal and every coordinatewise partial disturbance covariance has a positive-definite completion. The completion margin is computable from \(\chi_G(q)=\sup\{t:\exists K=K^{\mathsf T},\ \mathcal A_GK=q,\ K\succeq tI_m\}\), which is positive exactly for positive-definite completable data. Chordal graphs reduce to constructive maximal-clique tests, while a signed four-cycle proves that positive-definite edge blocks do not suffice for nonchordal graphs. With sourcewise-iid Gaussian samples for every observed edge and every marginal, simultaneous operator-norm regions invert to confidence sets for the graph-identified coefficient tuples; positive-definite edge-joint and marginal covariances, a fixed graph-feasibility margin excluding completion boundaries, and the path-product margin yield Hausdorff coefficient-set consistency and exact essential-poset recovery. A separate generic elbow proves that no paired block is insufficient whereas any one preassigned view pair generically identifies the full coefficient tuple. The memoized removed-set recursion supplies a \(2^p\)-state compatibility representation; no duplicate-free output-sensitive enumeration guarantee is claimed.

project_justification.gap: Existing multi-view LiMVAM identification results address full pairing under disturbance-diversity conditions, while Gaussian-DAG estimators target a point-identified DAG from one joint law. Neither line gives a complete population and finite-sample characterization for an arbitrary graph of paired views, where observed-edge residual diagonality and global positive-definite completion are separate requirements. General set-inference results also do not provide the graph-specific residual, completion-boundary, coefficient, and ancestral-path perturbation controls required here.
project_justification.niche: For the component-aligned Gaussian subclass, each candidate order fixes every view-specific coefficient matrix from its marginal covariance. Observed view edges then specify entries of each coordinatewise disturbance covariance, so global compatibility is measured by residual diagonality together with the computable semidefinite margin \(\chi_G\). This decomposition supports sourcewise covariance regions on an arbitrary view graph, needs no cross-source independence, and retains every participant or source marginal for coefficient estimation.
project_justification.fill: The graph-completion theorem proves necessity by restricting full disturbance covariances and sufficiency by independently completing the coordinatewise partial matrices. The identity \(\chi_G(q)>0\) if and only if \(q\) admits a positive-definite completion gives a computable feasibility side; its zero-fill perturbation bound combines with residual stability to control the graph violation score. A union bound over \(\lvert E_{\mathrm{obs}}\rvert+m\) Gaussian covariance sources yields simultaneous operator-norm coverage. Inverting this region covers the graph-identified tuple set, excludes graph-incompatible orders once the radius is small relative to the fixed feasibility margin, gives Hausdorff error at most \(2L_B\bar r_{G,n}\), and recovers the graph-essential poset under the path-product margin. Chordal maximal-clique completion, the nonchordal four-cycle obstruction, the generic one-pair elbow, and the \(2^p\)-state removed-set recursion complete the population and inference frontier asserted here.

body.related_work: HeurtebiseEtAl2026LiMVAM is the model anchor: its Section 4.6 uses edgewise cross-view correlation diversity to identify a partial order and view-specific coefficients under full pairing. The present results hold only for the narrower component-aligned Gaussian subclass and do not claim containment of the published Heurtebise class. ShimizuEtAl2011DirectLiNGAM and Shimizu2012JointLiNGAM motivate recursive residualization under non-Gaussianity, but they do not establish removed-set path independence or partial-view-graph covariance completion. ChenEtAl2024IndividualCausal and GhassamiEtAl2018MultiDomain pool population or domain information through ICA structure or heterogeneity rather than selected paired covariance blocks. HyttinenEberhardtHoyer2012Overlapping studies overlapping experimental total-effect measurements, not residual covariance restrictions among passive views. GroneEtAl1984PositiveDefiniteCompletion supplies the chordal maximal-clique completion theorem used by the graph specialization; the residual reduction, the \(\chi_G\) formulation, and the signed four-cycle obstruction are derived here. HauserBuhlmann2014ActiveLearning and LindgrenEtAl2018CostAware concern intervention-target design through separating systems, whereas the present calibration choice is passive observation of view-pair covariance blocks. GhoshalHonorio2018LinearSEM uses recursive Schur updates and score gaps in a point-identifying linear SEM. GaoTaiAragam2022GaussianDAG studies point-identifying Gaussian-DAG estimation rather than set-valued compatibility from a partially paired multi-view graph. Vershynin2018HighDimensionalProbability supplies Gaussian singular-value concentration, and ChernozhukovHongTamer2007SetInference supplies the general criterion-inversion comparison; neither gives the graph-specific completion and path-product perturbation argument. MohanPearl2021MissingData studies recoverability under missingness graphs, whereas the sourcewise-iid common-population design here assumes away selection and transport. TaylorEtAl2017CamCAN documents the motivating MEG and MRI cohort but does not validate component alignment or the graph-sampling assumptions. As a separate future-work direction, the class-enumeration paradigms of GuoPerkovic2021MinimalEffects, WienobstEtAl2023MECEnumeration, WangEtAl2023EquivalenceEnumeration, and AvisFukuda1996ReverseSearch might inform numerical-tuple deduplication, but none supplies such an algorithm for the present modified-Cholesky fibers.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The population and inference results remain confined to the component-aligned Gaussian subclass. For nonchordal view graphs, positive definiteness of every specified edge block is only necessary; the global completion margin \(\chi_G\) must still be computed. Finite-sample coverage requires every observed edge-joint covariance and every view marginal covariance to be positive definite so that all whitening inverses exist. Hausdorff set consistency and exact poset recovery require a fixed positive graph-feasibility margin, which explicitly excludes both residual-diagonality and positive-definite-completion boundary failures, together with a fixed path-product margin. The generic elbow is relative to a fixed-order finite-dimensional parameterization and gives no uniform distance from its exceptional algebraic set. The \(2^p\)-state recursion counts exact-real arithmetic rather than bit complexity, and it does not by itself certify output-sensitive numerical deduplication.
body.honest_scope: The arbitrary-view-graph completion theorem, graph covariance-region inversion, chordal specialization, nonchordal obstruction, generic calibration elbow, fixed-order recovery, removed-set recursion, essential poset, and minimum calibration statements concern only the component-aligned Gaussian subclass with positive-definite coordinate disturbance covariances. They do not transfer to unrestricted LiMVAMs or establish the assumptions used by Heurtebise et al. Finite-sample graph inversion additionally requires sourcewise-iid same-population Gaussian sampling, positive-definite edge-joint and marginal covariances, a positive graph-feasibility margin away from completion boundaries, and a positive path-product margin; it assumes neither cross-source independence nor selection or transport. Genericity is relative to coefficients respecting a fixed common order and supplies no uniform identification margin. Cam-CAN MEG and fMRI remain prospective diagnostic applications rather than empirical validation. The algorithmic guarantee delivered by the recursion is the memoized \(2^p\)-state compatibility construction, not exact-once output-sensitive enumeration of distinct numerical tuples.
